notes.meaning: God commands Moses to announce the sacred calendar to the people of Israel. These special times belong to the Lord Himself, and the priests were to call the whole nation together to worship Him. God calls His people to step away from daily routines to focus on who He is and what He has done.

God places the weekly Sabbath at the start of all sacred times. On the seventh day, the people had to stop all ordinary work and gather for rest and worship wherever they lived. This weekly pause reminded the people that their time, work, and lives belong entirely to God.

differ.view: Christians are free from keeping any specific day of rest, since Christ has fulfilled the Sabbath and gives spiritual rest every day.
The moral duty to set aside one day in seven for rest and public worship remains binding, observed on the Lord's Day (Sunday).

notes.meaning: God introduces the annual festivals that occur at fixed times each year, as distinct from the weekly Sabbath. The priests announced these holy days with the blast of trumpets so families across the land could prepare. Each festival served as an appointed meeting between God and His people.

Passover is set for twilight on the fourteenth day of the first month, which falls in early spring. Families remembered the night God spared their ancestors from death in Egypt through the blood of a lamb. For Christians, this points to Jesus, the true Passover Lamb whose death rescues us from sin.

The Feast of Unleavened Bread begins the very next day and lasts for seven days. The people were forbidden to eat bread made with yeast, recalling how quickly Israel had to leave Egypt without waiting for dough to rise. Because yeast spreads and swells, getting rid of it also pictured turning away from sin and living a pure life.

The first and last days of the festival were special days of worship when ordinary job-related labor stopped. People were still permitted to prepare daily food, but heavy field work and trade ceased. Special animal sacrifices were offered on the altar each day to show ongoing devotion to God.

God looks ahead to the day Israel enters the Promised Land and begins farming. Before harvesting the fields for their own food, they were to bring the first bundle of ripe barley to the priest. Giving God the firstfruits—the very first portion of the crop—showed trust that the entire harvest was a gift from Him.

The priest presented the grain by waving it back and forth before the Lord on the day after the Sabbath. This ceremony dedicated the coming harvest to God so the people could enjoy the rest with His favor. Christians see this Sunday wave offering as a picture of Jesus rising from the dead as the firstfruits of new life.

Along with the grain, the priest offered a healthy year-old male lamb as a burnt offering, expressing complete surrender to God. A generous grain offering mixed with olive oil and a cup of wine accompanied the animal. This double portion of flour showed extra thanksgiving for the land's rich harvest.

The people were forbidden to eat any bread, roasted kernels, or fresh grain from the new crop until this offering was made. Acknowledging God's provision had to come before enjoying the blessing. This lasting rule taught every generation to honor God first with their income and food.

Starting from the day the first sheaf was waved, the people counted off seven full weeks, or forty-nine days. On the fiftieth day, known later as Pentecost, they celebrated the Feast of Weeks at the end of the wheat harvest. A brand-new grain offering was brought to thank God for bringing the spring crops to full maturity.

The people brought two loaves of fine wheat flour baked with yeast to wave before the Lord. Unlike altar offerings where yeast was forbidden, these loaves represented the ordinary daily bread eaten in Israeli homes. Waving them acknowledged that God provides everyday food for our families.

A large group of animal sacrifices accompanied the two loaves, including seven lambs, a young bull, two rams, a goat, and two additional lambs. These sacrifices included burnt offerings of dedication, a sin offering for national cleansing, and peace offerings celebrating fellowship with God. Together, they covered the full range of worship, moving from confession of sin to joyful communion.

The priest waved the two peace-offering lambs alongside the two loaves of bread before the Lord. After being presented to God, these items were set apart as sacred food for the officiating priests. God sustained the ministers who served His house through the grateful worship of His people.

On this fiftieth day, the priests sounded trumpets to gather the community for worship, and all regular daily labor stopped. Later Jewish tradition celebrated this day as the anniversary of the giving of the Law at Mount Sinai. In the New Testament, God chose this exact festival to pour out the Holy Spirit on the early church in Jerusalem.

When harvesting their crops, landowners were ordered to leave the corners of their fields uncut and not pick up fallen grain. These gleanings were left for poor neighbors and foreign travelers who owned no land. True gratitude toward God always leads to practical kindness and generosity toward people in need.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars often regard this verse as an editorial insertion from chapter 19, placed here to anchor social welfare rules directly within harvest celebrations.
